posts.content_md:
Ok, I didn't know how to present this but I think I may be able to find the words. I don't have the equiptment necessary to perform the tests but thought I would throw it out there.

Take two solutions of gelatin and water. One at 100ml water and 10g of gelatin and the other 100ml of water and 12g of gelatin at 120F and pour them on plates and spin them at the same speed for x minutes. I assume the viscosity of the two are nearly identical and would yield a final wet thickness nearly the same. Then let the plates dry.

Do the properties of the gelatin only allow it to bond and compact at a certain density such that the higher concentration solution dries thicker and retains more water but the density of the gelatin is the same per cubic area. Or will the higher density gelatin solution give up the same amount of water as the lower concentration solution and thus have a higher concentration of gelatin per cubic area after dry.

Then, do the two dry at different rates, even thought the wet thicknesses are the same? That is, does it take the same time to get 60% of the water to evaportate out of each?

Good question John for the viscosity and spin coating aspect.

I am sure you have the equipment to do the experiment OK. 

Just do the 2 solutions on 2 **pre-weighed**plates and then keep weighing them separately until they each get to a constant weight. (using an overnite warmer etc. )My guess is that the "12g" one will finish up with more gelatin than the "10g" one. I'll contribute another $20 to Colin's Forum fund if I'm wrong!

If you have cut the plates as good rectangles you can also work out the thickness of gelatin from the area and density (specific gravity ) of the dry gelatin I guess.

We can all theorize till the cows come home, let's see what actually happens.

> My guess is that the 12g one will finish up with more gelatin than the 10g one

I agree but does the one with the higher gelatin concentration maintain a thicker coating after a period of 1 hour, 4 hours, 24 hours as compared to the one with less gelatin even thought they started seconds after coating at the same thickness? And does the one with a higher gelatin concentration contain more water after those intervals of time compared to the one with less gelatin? I guess the latter question could be answered with weight if I had a very accurate scale, which I do not. The first question needs to be addressed with a very accurate thickness measurement, which also I do not have.

Also, If I allow both solution with different concentraton of gelatin to become equal weight then the one with more gelatin would have to have lost more water to account for the additional weight of the extra gelatin, no? 

I am not sure why you state I have the equipment. I thought I stated I did not. I assume I would need a scale that can measure take 50 or 100 grams with increments as small as a few micrograms. And the only thickness measurement tool I have is a C type micrometer which I do not beleive is useful until the gelatin is completely dry and hard, otherwise a mechanical measurement will deform the gelatin.

I may play with what I have and see if I can determine anything but it was more of a thought problem and thought provoker then asking what I can expect as results. I am just trying to gain the full picture of what goes on at the micro level in a gelatin solution.
